questions.question: What is a database?
questions.answer: A database is a digital storage system that stores data so it can be efficiently saved, retrieved, updated, and deleted. Unlike Excel or paper registers, databases support security, multi-user access, automation, and scalability.

questions.question: What is a DBMS, and how is it different from a database?
questions.answer: A database is the place where data is physically stored. A DBMS (Database Management System) is the software that creates, manages, secures, and optimizes that database. Example: MySQL is a DBMS; the 'college' database you create inside MySQL is the database.

questions.question: What is SQL?
questions.answer: SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is the standard language used to communicate with relational databases — to create structures, insert data, retrieve data, update records, delete records, and manage permissions.

questions.question: What are the three types of data? Give an example of each.
questions.answer: 1) Structured data — organized in fixed rows and columns, e.g., a student table in MySQL. 2) Semi-structured data — not in table format but has internal structure, e.g., a JSON or XML file. 3) Unstructured data — no defined format, e.g., images, videos, audio files, and raw PDFs.

questions.question: What are the four SQL command categories? Give one command per category.
questions.answer: 1) DDL (Data Definition Language) — CREATE (creates tables/databases). 2) DML (Data Manipulation Language) — INSERT (adds data to tables). 3) DQL (Data Query Language) — SELECT (retrieves data). 4) DCL (Data Control Language) — GRANT (gives user permissions). TCL (Transaction Control Language) is sometimes listed as a fifth category — COMMIT saves changes permanently.

questions.question: Why does a SQL statement need to end with a semicolon?
questions.answer: The semicolon is the statement terminator. It tells the SQL engine that the command is complete and should now be executed. Without it in the CLI, the engine waits thinking you are still typing. Some GUI tools add it automatically, but it is always required in the terminal.

questions.question: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
questions.answer: DELETE is a DML command that removes rows one at a time and logs each deletion — it can be used with WHERE to target specific rows. TRUNCATE is a DDL command that removes all rows at once extremely fast without logging individual rows. TRUNCATE cannot be used with a WHERE clause and cannot be rolled back in most databases.

questions.question: What is a PRIMARY KEY?
questions.answer: A PRIMARY KEY is a column (or set of columns) that uniquely identifies each record in a table. It must be unique — no two rows can have the same value — and it cannot be NULL. For example, a student id column set as PRIMARY KEY ensures every student has a distinct identifier.

questions.question: What is the difference between RDBMS and NoSQL databases?
questions.answer: RDBMS (Relational Database Management System) stores structured data in tables with fixed columns and uses SQL. Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle. NoSQL databases are designed for semi-structured or unstructured data with flexible schemas. They come in four types: Document (MongoDB), Key-Value (Redis), Column (Cassandra), and Graph (Neo4j).

questions.question: What are the eight problems with using Excel or registers for college data management?
questions.answer: 1) No security — anyone can open, edit, or delete. 2) No multi-user access — concurrent edits corrupt data. 3) Slow searching — manual lookups in thousands of rows. 4) No relationships — data in separate files can become inconsistent. 5) No automation — cannot auto-calculate or trigger actions. 6) Cannot handle big data — crashes with millions of records. 7) No backup and recovery — data lost if file is deleted. 8) Reporting is slow and error-prone.

questions.question: Describe a situation where INNER JOIN would return fewer results than LEFT JOIN.
questions.answer: (Situation) I had a students table and a departments table. Some students were assigned to CIVIL, which did not exist in the departments table. (Task) I needed to produce a report of all students with their department head. (Action) I first tested INNER JOIN — it excluded all CIVIL students because there was no match in departments. I then switched to LEFT JOIN with students as the left table. (Result) LEFT JOIN returned all students including CIVIL students, showing NULL in the hod_name column. LEFT JOIN was the correct choice to avoid data loss.

questions.question: A team member ran DELETE FROM students; without a WHERE clause. What happened and how would you prevent it?
questions.answer: (Situation) All rows in the students table were wiped. DELETE without WHERE removes every single row — the table structure remains but all data is gone. (Task) Recover the data and prevent recurrence. (Action) Restored from the latest DBMS backup. Implemented a policy requiring WHERE clauses in all DELETE statements. Enabled safe mode in MySQL which prevents DELETE/UPDATE without WHERE. (Result) Data was recovered and the same mistake was prevented going forward. Always use WHERE with DELETE.

questions.question: How would you set up MySQL on a new Ubuntu EC2 instance for a web application?
questions.answer: (Situation) A new EC2 Ubuntu server needed a MySQL database for a Node.js application. (Task) Install and securely configure MySQL. (Action) 1) sudo apt update && sudo apt install mysql-server -y. 2) sudo mysql_secure_installation to set root password and remove anonymous accounts. 3) Fixed Ubuntu's auth_socket issue with ALTER USER to set password-based login. 4) Created the application database with CREATE DATABASE myapp. 5) Created a dedicated app user with CREATE USER 'appuser'@'%' and GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON myapp.*. 6) Opened port 3306 in the EC2 Security Group. (Result) MySQL was running, secured, and accessible to the application server.

questions.question: A manager asks: 'Which departments have more than 10 students? Show me only those.' Write the query and explain.
questions.answer: (Situation) Raw student data exists in a students table with a department column. (Task) Filter departments by student count. (Action) Query: SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*) > 10; GROUP BY groups students by department. COUNT(*) counts students per group. HAVING filters groups — only those with more than 10 students are returned. WHERE cannot be used here because it filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters after grouping. (Result) Only departments with more than 10 students appear in the output.

questions.question: Why should the MySQL root account never be used for application database connections?
questions.answer: (Situation) A developer suggested using root credentials in the app's database connection string to simplify setup. (Task) Explain the security risk and propose a safer approach. (Action) Root has ALL PRIVILEGES over the entire MySQL server — not just one database. If the application is ever compromised (SQL injection, credential leak), an attacker with root can destroy all databases, create backdoor users, or dump all data. Instead, create a dedicated user: CREATE USER 'appuser'@'<app-ip>' IDENTIFIED BY 'SecurePass!'; GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON myapp.* TO 'appuser'@'<app-ip>'; This limits the user to only the myapp database. (Result) Even if credentials are leaked, the attacker can only access one database — not the whole server.

questions.question: A query with WHERE department = 'CSE' is used but you also need to count students per department. Will this work?
questions.answer: (Situation) Combining WHERE with GROUP BY in a query. (Task) Count students per department but only for CSE. (Action) SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM students WHERE department = 'CSE' GROUP BY department; WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping — only CSE rows remain. GROUP BY then groups those rows. COUNT(*) counts them. This works fine. WHERE filters individual rows. HAVING filters aggregated groups. For filtering by a non-aggregated condition before grouping, WHERE is correct. (Result) The query correctly returns the count of CSE students.

questions.question: What is the difference between MySQL's bind-address = 127.0.0.1 and bind-address = 0.0.0.0?
questions.answer: (Situation) After installing MySQL and creating a remote user, a developer cannot connect from another machine. (Task) Diagnose and fix the connectivity issue. (Action) The default bind-address = 127.0.0.1 means MySQL only listens on the local loopback interface — no external connections are accepted at all. Changed to bind-address = 0.0.0.0 in /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf. This makes MySQL listen on all available network interfaces. Also opened port 3306 in the EC2 Security Group with the app server's private IP as the source. (Result) Remote MySQL connection successful.

questions.question: When would you use a FULL OUTER JOIN?
questions.answer: (Situation) Two tables — students and departments — have data that does not fully overlap. Some students belong to departments not listed in the departments table. Some departments have no enrolled students. (Task) Produce a complete report that shows all students AND all departments without losing any data. (Action) FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables. Unmatched rows on either side show NULL for the missing columns. In MySQL, FULL JOIN is not directly supported — simulate using LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT JOIN. (Result) The report shows all students including those with missing departments AND all departments including those with no students.

questions.question: What is a SELF JOIN and when would you use it?
questions.answer: (Situation) A single students table contains student names and their departments. (Task) Find all pairs of students who are in the same department. (Action) Use a SELF JOIN — the same table is joined with itself using two different aliases: SELECT a.name AS student1, b.name AS student2, a.department FROM students a JOIN students b ON a.department = b.department AND a.id <> b.id; The condition a.id <> b.id prevents matching a student with themselves. (Result) All pairs of students sharing the same department are listed.

questions.question: How does DBMS concurrency control solve the multi-user access problem?
questions.answer: (Situation) A college uses Excel for attendance. Two teachers open the same file and edit it simultaneously — one teacher's changes overwrite the other's. (Task) Replace with a system that handles concurrent edits safely. (Action) DBMS concurrency control uses locking mechanisms and transaction isolation. When Teacher A updates attendance for Roll 101, DBMS locks that row. Teacher B's update for Roll 102 proceeds independently. No conflict occurs. Multiple transactions run simultaneously but are isolated from each other. (Result) Data integrity is maintained even with hundreds of simultaneous users.

questions.question: Explain the complete SQL query execution order.
questions.answer: SQL queries are written in a specific order but executed by the engine in a different sequence. Written order: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Execution order: 1) FROM — identify the table. 2) WHERE — filter rows. 3) GROUP BY — group the filtered rows. 4) HAVING — filter groups. 5) SELECT — compute what to return. 6) ORDER BY — sort results. 7) LIMIT — restrict rows returned. This explains why HAVING can use aggregate functions (applied after grouping) but WHERE cannot (applied before grouping).

questions.question: When would you choose NoSQL over RDBMS?
questions.answer: Choose NoSQL when: 1) Data is semi-structured or unstructured (e.g., JSON documents, media files). 2) Schema changes frequently — NoSQL allows flexible, schema-less data. 3) Horizontal scaling is needed — NoSQL databases scale across many servers easily. 4) High write throughput is required — document and key-value stores are optimized for this. 5) Graph relationships are needed — graph databases (Neo4j) are optimized for relationship traversal. Choose RDBMS when data is structured, relationships between tables are important, and ACID compliance is critical (financial transactions, student records).

questions.question: What is the difference between COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT?
questions.answer: All three are TCL (Transaction Control Language) commands that manage database transactions. COMMIT permanently saves all DML changes made since the last commit. Once committed, changes cannot be undone. ROLLBACK undoes all uncommitted DML changes — restoring data to the state at the last COMMIT or SAVEPOINT. SAVEPOINT creates a named checkpoint within a transaction. You can ROLLBACK to a specific SAVEPOINT without undoing the entire transaction. Together they ensure safe, atomic operations — if one step fails, the whole transaction can be rolled back.

questions.question: Explain database indexing and why it matters for performance.
questions.answer: An index in a database is a separate data structure that speeds up data retrieval — similar to a book's index at the back. Without an index, SQL must scan every row sequentially (full table scan) to find matching records. With an index on a column (e.g., student_id), the engine jumps directly to relevant rows. Indexes dramatically speed up SELECT queries, especially on large tables. The trade-off: indexes consume extra storage and slow down INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations since the index must also be updated. Always index columns used frequently in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY clauses.

questions.question: What is the difference between Cloud-Native DBMS and traditional DBMS?
questions.answer: Traditional DBMS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle) requires manual installation, configuration, patching, scaling, and backup management on a server you manage. Cloud-Native DBMS (AWS RDS, DynamoDB, Azure CosmosDB) is a fully managed service — the cloud provider handles installation, patching, automatic backups, scaling, high availability, and failover. Benefits of cloud-native: no server management, automatic multi-AZ replication, point-in-time recovery, and pay-as-you-go pricing. AWS RDS, for example, can run MySQL or PostgreSQL engines while fully automating all operational tasks. Trade-off: less control over fine-grained configuration.
